content: The term rectum implies a straight structure; however, the human rectum is not straight. It contains permanent transverse folds, which are semilunar in shape and are referred to as Houston’s valves or the transverse folds of the rectum. These folds project into the lumen of the rectum and measure approximately 12 mm in width. They are composed of some of the circular muscle fibers of the gut wall. When the rectum is empty, these folds overlap one another so effectively that significant maneuvering is required to pass a bougie or a finger through the rectal canal, as noted by Houston. The primary function of these folds appears to be the support of fecal matter, preventing its premature descent toward the anus. This is important because the presence of fecal matter in the anal canal triggers a sensation that demands its evacuation. Structurally, these folds are formed from the circular muscle layer of the rectal wall. Typically, there are three such folds, although variations exist where a fourth fold may be present, or occasionally only two are observed. The first fold is located near the beginning of the rectum on the right side. The second fold extends inward from the left side of the rectal tube, opposite the middle of the sacrum. The third fold, which is the largest and most consistent, projects backward from the anterior part of the rectum, opposite the fundus of the urinary bladder. This third fold is situated approximately 5 cm above the anus on the left and posterior wall of the rectal tube. From a clinical perspective, these folds are significant during procedures such as sigmoidoscopy and colonoscopy. During these examinations, the endoscope must be carefully maneuvered around these folds to navigate the rectal canal effectively.
